01_hook:
In the monsoon,
the rivers of the Peshawar Valley
rise and fall under thick cloud.

Optical satellites often
see only the cloud.

This is SARtale:
nine passes of the NASA-ISRO

NISAR satellite,
from July to October 2026,
What changed, when did it change,
and how far can we trust the answer?
02_radar:
NISAR sends microwave pulses down
and measures what comes back.

Calm water acts like a mirror
and sends the energy away,

Rough ground and buildings
scatter energy back,

We express gamma-zero backscatter
in decibels:

A rise of ten decibels means
ten times the power.

HH sends horizontal
and receives horizontal.

HV sends horizontal
and receives vertical.

They respond differently,
and that will matter.
03_curve:
Pick one place: the south-east shore
of Tarbela Reservoir.

In July, HH sits around
minus seven decibels.

By the nineteenth of August,
it has fallen to minus sixteen point six.
The obvious idea is to compare each date

with the median
of the other eligible dates.

Most of the season is dark,
so dark becomes normal,
and the big August change barely scores.
04_step: So we ask a better question.
Suppose there was one moment of change.

and take the mean before
and the mean after.
The gap between them is the step.
Now slide that split across the season,
keeping at least two dates on each side.

A big gap means little
if the points are noisy,

so we divide by how much they scatter
around their own means,

adjusted for how many dates
sit on each side.
For this shore, the best split falls

between the twenty-sixth of July
and the nineteenth of August:

a step of about
minus eight decibels in HH,

minus five in HV,
with a stability near six.
05_rule:
A pixel is flagged
only when three things hold.
HH and HV must move the same way.

Their average absolute step
must be at least three decibels.

And their combined stability
must be at least three.
The map groups pixels into cells

coloured by the most common
flagged step date and direction.
06_shuffle:
Choosing the best of several splits
inflates the scores, so we test it.

Shuffle the dates at each pixel
and run everything again.

The real order flags
1.39 percent of the map.

Shuffling the whole scene together,
two hundred times,

nothing flagged at Peshawar city
or in the main Tarbela pool

One caution: the rule was set
with the known sites in view,
so this was not a blind test.
07_missed:
Honest work also shows
what it cannot see.

HV jumped about fourteen decibels
over the west of the map,

so the date is left out
of the change analysis.
The highest listed flow at Nowshera,

came on the twenty-third of July,
between two passes.
And NISAR has a permanent data gap

from the twenty-seventh of July
to the tenth of August.
08a_app_open:
It opens on the finding,
with the real radar image behind it.

and ten guided steps
move the map to each place.
08b_app_dance:
Leave the story at any time
and explore freely.

Step through the dates,
switch between HH and HV,

and compare any two passes
with a before and after slider.
08c_app_change: Turn on Change to see the step map.

Light tints went brighter,
and deep shades went darker.
The key sits beside the map.
08d_app_sites: Site Stories puts the real curve first.

Every card separates what was observed
from the hypothesis,
what would test it, and its limits.
08e_app_evidence:
What NISAR Missed shows
every pass and the gap.

And How We Know sets out the data,
the method, the checks and the limits.
09_close: A step is not a cause.

Plain ground flags too,
and we do not yet know why.

The data is provisional,
and this is not a warning service.
But in one season of open NASA data,

we can show what radar saw,
when it changed,
and how much to trust it.

This is SARtale,
by team SARcastic Scientists.
